l: Xanthippus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Xanthippus, a Spartan hired by the Carthaginians as their general, arrived from Greece and enabled them to totally rout the Romans in Africa and destroy their numerous army.

l: Panormus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: The Romans sailed to Panormus after withdrawing from Drepanum, landed their army, and surrounded the city with walls and trenches. They breached the walls, freed forty thousand inhabitants who paid the agreed ransom, and sold thirty thousand others as slaves. Later, Asdrubal encamped near Panormus and was defeated there by Cecilius.

l: Asdrubal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Asdrubal, the Carthaginian general, marched to Panormus after being criticized by his soldiers for not fighting. He encamped close to the walls without fortifying his position, and Cecilius defeated his army while the soldiers were drunk; sixty elephants were captured.

l: Cecilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Cecilius, the Roman consul, attacked Asdrubal's Carthaginian army at Panormus while its soldiers were disorderly and drunk. He totally routed them and sent sixty captured elephants to Rome.

l: First Punic War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: The unit presents the war between Rome and Carthage through their campaigns in Sicily, Africa, and at sea. It includes the siege of Messana, the capture and destruction of Sicilian cities, the Roman defeat in Africa, and major naval disasters.

l: siege of Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: Hiero and the Carthaginians jointly besieged Messana after making an agreement to attack the Romans unless they withdrew from Sicily. Rome sent Appius Claudius with a large army, and the Roman intervention led Hiero to abandon the siege and flee to Syracuse.

l: siege of Agrigentum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: The Romans besieged Agrigentum with an army said to number one hundred thousand men. After stout resistance, the Carthaginians surrendered the city to Rome, though Carthaginian forces later recaptured, burned, and demolished it after a Roman naval disaster.

l: Roman defeat by Xantippos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: A Roman army under the consul Attilius initially defeated the Carthaginians and captured many towns and castles in Africa. After Xanthippus the Spartan took command of the Carthaginians, they totally routed the Romans and destroyed the army.

l: Roman naval shipwreck at Camarina, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIIL
s: After defeating the Carthaginians at sea and capturing twenty-four ships, the Romans were shipwrecked near Camarina while sailing toward Sicily. They lost three hundred and forty warships, numerous transport vessels, and many men and horses; Hiero aided the survivors and conveyed them safely to Messana.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The unit recounts the Roman siege of Lilybaeum during the long war with Carthage, including naval battles, failed blockades, military losses, and the eventual peace after twenty-four years. It then describes Carthaginian expansion in Spain under Amilcar and Asdrubal, the rise of Hannibal, and the destruction of Saguntum that led to the Hannibalic War. It also includes observations about religious and moral life, military discipline, leadership, and the destructive effects of envy and luxury.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Carthaginians defended Lilybaeum, repeatedly relieved the city with troops and provisions, and destroyed or defeated Roman forces at sea and on land. They later expanded in Spain under Amilcar, Asdrubal, and Hannibal.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Romans besieged Lilybaeum but suffered severe losses through failed fortifications, disease, shortages, and naval defeats. They eventually concluded a peace with the Carthaginians after the war had lasted twenty-four years.

l: Lilybaeum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Lilybaeum was the city besieged by the Romans after the Carthaginians moved citizens there from SeltnqS|». The city was repeatedly supplied and defended by the Carthaginians.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Carthage sent troops, corn, provisions, and fleets to relieve Lilybaeum. It later sent forces against the Numidians and selected Hannibal as general.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Sicily was the setting for the siege of Lilybaeum, the naval battles near Drepanum and Gela, and the conflicts involving Syracuse, Eryx, and other places.

l: Lilybaeum siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Romans surrounded Lilybaeum with trenches, engines, batteries, and attempted harbor blockades. Carthaginian sorties and relief efforts repeatedly damaged the Roman works, while Roman naval defeats and shortages brought the siege close to failure before peace was made.

l: Roman fleet, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Roman fleet suffered repeated disasters. Claudius lost 117 ships and 20,000 men near Drepanum, and another Roman fleet later lost 105 long galleys and nearly all its transport ships in a storm near Camarina.

l: Roman army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Roman army at Lilybaeum numbered 110,000 men, including 60,000 infantry and 700 cavalry. It endured the destruction of its engines, shortages, disease, and the loss of thousands of men.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Syracuse was associated with Hiero, who supplied the Romans with corn. Junius sailed toward Syracuse hoping to receive help after the Roman fleet's defeat.

l: Carthalo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Carthalo commanded Carthaginian naval forces. He relieved Lilybaeum, attacked Roman shipping, defeated Roman fleets, and later captured the castle of Igotbalus.

l: Drepanum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Drepanum received the Carthaginian cavalry sent away from Lilybaeum and served as a destination for captured provisions. The major naval defeat of Claudius also occurred near Drepanum.

l: First Punic War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The conflict described between the Romans and Carthaginians lasted twenty-four years, while Lilybaeum was besieged for ten years, and ended with a mutually concluded peace.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Diodorus Siculus is identified in the headings as the author associated with the historical fragments in this unit.

l: Carthaginian mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: After leaving Sicily, the Carthaginian mercenaries rebelled because they considered their demands for the horses and men lost in Sicily unreasonable and excessive. They fought one another for four years and four months before being put to death by Barcas.

l: Spaniards, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Spaniards were brought under the authority of Asdrubal, who gained cities in Spain, married the daughter of the king of Spain, and received full governmental power from the Spaniards.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Amilcar expanded Carthaginian power toward the Pillars of Hercules and Gades, subdued Iberians, Tartessians, and Celts, and gained many cities in Spain. He founded Acra Leuca and was drowned while fleeing across a river after raising the siege of Helice.

l: Acra Leuca, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Acra Leuca was a large town built by Amilcar in Spain and named for its situation. Hannibal and Asdrubal reached it safely after Amilcar's death, and Asdrubal later used it as a base.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Hannibal, the eldest son of Amilcar, was unanimously chosen general of the Carthaginians after Asdrubal was slain. He besieged and captured Saguntum, an event that led to the Hannibalic War.

l: Asdrubal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Asdrubal, Amilcar's son-in-law, defeated the forces of King Orissus, took twelve cities, and brought all the cities of Spain under his control. He was later assassinated by one of his household after serving as general for nine years.

l: Saguntum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: Saguntum was besieged and captured by Hannibal. Its citizens destroyed or rendered useless their wealth, made a final sally, and died fighting rather than leave useful plunder to Hannibal.

l: Hannibal's siege of Saguntum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: During Hannibal's siege of Saguntum, the citizens melted down their gold and silver with brass and lead, then fought to the last person. The mothers killed their children and themselves, so Hannibal gained the town without benefiting from its plunder.

l: Hannibalic War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, vooKxxiy.
s: The Hannibalic War began when the Romans, unable to obtain a trial of Hannibal for violating the league after the capture of Saguntum, started the war.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Rhodian ambassadors came to Rome to seek pardon for appearing to favor Perseus during the war with him, and they were reproved and fined but relieved of their fears. Perseus, the last king of Macedonia, was captured by Aemilius, confined in the prison of Alba, and later died after being transferred to a less severe confinement. The unit traces the Cappadocian royal genealogy from Cyrus through Ariarathes and describes several alleged cases of people whose bodily characteristics were interpreted as those of both sexes. It also recounts the destruction of Carthage, the endurance and prosperity of Masinissa, and the violent seizure of the Bithynian kingdom by Nicomedes after killing Prusias.

l: Rhodians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The Rhodians sent ambassadors to Rome to beg pardon for appearing to favor Perseus and for breaking their league with the Romans during the war. Their embassy failed to obtain everything it sought, but the senate's answer relieved their fears; they were sharply reproved and fined.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Rome received the Rhodian ambassadors and judged their conduct during the war with Perseus. Its senate is presented as encouraging leading men to compete in generosity and public service rather than envy one another.

l: Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Perseus, the last king of Macedonia, was captured by Aemilius after repeatedly opposing the Romans in the field, and Aemilius celebrated a triumph after the victory. Perseus was confined in the prison of Alba, later moved to a milder confinement through the intervention of Marcus Aemilius, and eventually died after his keeper deprived him of sleep.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The Romans are described as praising and commending one another when pursuing the public good. Their valor and engines overcame the defenses of Carthage, and their natural humanity was invoked when the senate reconsidered Perseus's harsh confinement.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Macedonia is identified as the kingdom ruled by Perseus, its last king, before his defeat and capture by Aemilius.

l: Macedonian War with Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: During the war with Perseus, the Rhodians were thought to have favored the king and broken their league with Rome. The war ended with Perseus's capture and Aemilius's triumph.

l: Cappadocia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Cappadocia was brought under Macedonian control after Eumenes defeated and killed Ariarathes, but Ariarathes, the adopted heir, later recovered the kingdom with Armenian assistance. Under a later Ariarathes, Cappadocia became attractive to learned Greeks, and its ruler renewed peace and friendship with the Romans.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The kings of Cappadocia claimed descent from Cyrus through Atossa, whom they identified as Cyrus's daughter. Their royal genealogy was traced down from Cyrus through several generations to the Cappadocian kings.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The Cappadocian kings also claimed descent from one of the seven Persians who killed Magus. Anaphas is described as a member of that group and as a man who abdicated the government of Cappadocia rather than pay tribute to the Persians.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The Persians fought Ditamus, who was killed while resisting them, and later fought alongside Ariarathes against the Egyptians. The Cappadocian genealogy claimed descent from one of the seven Persians who killed Magus.

l: Ariarathes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Several rulers named Ariarathes appear in the Cappadocian genealogy. One was killed by Eumenes, while the adopted Ariarathes fled to Armenia and later recovered Cappadocia; a later Ariarathes became co-ruler with his father and then ruled alone, and another succeeded to the kingdom as a young child.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Alexander the Macedonian king is said to have ruined the Persian empire and died soon afterward. In another account, Alexander fled from battle with five hundred men to Abas in Arabia and had previously entrusted his young son Antiochus to Diodes.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Perdiccas, who held the chief command after Alexander's death, sent Eumenes into Cappadocia. He is said to have died not long afterward while Antigonus and Seleucus were involved in war.

l: Arabia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Arabia contained the city of Abas, where Alexander fled after a battle and where the unusual person later called Diophantus was born.

l: Abas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Abas was a city in Arabia ruled by Diodes. Alexander fled there with five hundred men, and it was also the place where Diophantus was born and where the king later stayed.

l: Diophantus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Diophantus was first the name of a Macedonian living in Abas and later became the name assumed by his child after the child was publicly recognized as male. The person served in the king's cavalry and resided with the king at Abas.

l: Heracles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The account concerns a person called Heraldes, the daughter of Diophantus, whose body developed male genital features after an illness. After the discovery, that person adopted male clothing and was later called Diophantus.

l: Semiades, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Semiades married Heraldes and later returned to claim the spouse. After the bodily condition was revealed in court, he left his goods to Diophantus, made Diophantus his heir, and died from grief and shame.

l: Callo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Callo was an orphaned young woman in Epidauros who lacked a normal genital passage but had an opening through which urine passed. After an apothecary surgically exposed and repaired male genital organs, Callo abandoned feminine occupations and took the name Gallon.

l: hermaphrodites, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The text describes alleged hermaphrodites as people whose bodily formation could give observers the impression that both sexes were present, while rejecting the claim that both sexes were naturally formed together in one body. It says that superstition led to the burning of such people at Rome and Athens, and it denies stories that they could alternate sexual functions.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Carthage was said to have walls forty cubits high and twenty-two cubits broad. Despite its defenses, the Romans captured the city and razed it to the ground.

l: Masinissa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Masinissa, called Manasses by the text, ruled in Africa and remained a friend of the Romans. He lived ninety years in strength and good health, reigned for sixty years, left ten sons under Roman guardianship, and distributed extensive, well-equipped farmland among them.

l: Nicomedes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Nicomedes routed his father Prusias and forced him to flee for shelter to the temple of Jupiter. He then killed Prusias there and obtained the kingdom through that act.

l: Prusias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: Prusias was defeated by his son Nicomedes and fled to the temple of Jupiter for protection. Nicomedes killed him there and seized the kingdom.

l: Cappadocian royal genealogy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXI.
s: The Cappadocian royal genealogy claims descent from Cyrus and from one of the seven Persians who killed Magus. It traces the succession through Anaphas, Ditamus, Ariamenes, Ariarathes, and later rulers, including the adopted Ariarathes who recovered the kingdom after Macedonian conquest.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: The Lusitanians were initially easily defeated by the Romans because they lacked an experienced general, but they later caused the Romans serious trouble under Viriathus. Viriathus, formerly a shepherd known for his strength, endurance, and fighting ability, became their general and won several battles, including victories over Vitellius and Fabius. After Ceepio repeatedly defeated Viriathus and Viriathus sued for peace, Ceepio arranged for his assassination by some of his own servants. Ceepio then intimidated Tantalus and his army, imposed terms on them, and gave them a city and surrounding land as their habitation.

l: Lusitanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: The Lusitanians were initially easily vanquished by the Romans because they lacked an expert general. Under Viriathus, they won several battles against the Romans, but after Viriathus's death they were intimidated by Ceepio and accepted the terms he imposed.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: The Romans easily defeated the Lusitanians at first. Viriathus later caused them much harm, defeated their forces in several battles, and forced Fabius to accept dishonourable terms.

l: Viriathus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Viriathus had been a shepherd from childhood and was exceptionally strong and agile because of his sparse diet, hard labour, and disciplined sleep. After becoming general, he led the Lusitanians successfully, distributed spoils fairly, defeated Vitellius, and forced Fabius to accept dishonourable terms. Ceepio later defeated him repeatedly, and Viriathus sued for peace before being treacherously assassinated.

l: Vitellius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Vitellius was the Roman general whom Viriathus routed. Viriathus broke his army, took him prisoner, and put him to death.

l: Fabius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Fabius was appointed general against Viriathus, after which Viriathus began to decline. Viriathus later rallied his men and managed the conflict so successfully that he forced Fabius to accept terms dishonourable to the Romans.

l: Ceepio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Ceepio became general against Viriathus and rejected the former conditions as having no effect. He often defeated Viriathus, caused him to sue for peace, arranged his treacherous assassination, and then imposed whatever terms he pleased on Tantalus and his army.

l: battles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Viriathus was successful in many battles and gained admiration for his military conduct. He defeated Vitellius and later fought Fabius, whom he forced to accept dishonourable terms; Ceepio subsequently often defeated Viriathus.

l: Viriathus becoming general, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: After Viriathus became general, a group of thieves and rogues suddenly gathered around him. His success in many battles, fair distribution of spoils, and military conduct led him to appear more like a prince than a thief or robber.

l: Viriathus's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Viriathus's men were rallied after he began to decline, and he used them effectively against Fabius. Ceepio later struck terror into Tantalus and his army and imposed terms upon them.

l: peace terms, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: Viriathus forced Fabius to accept terms dishonourable to the Romans. Ceepio disregarded those former conditions, and after Viriathus's death imposed whatever terms he pleased on Tantalus and his army, ultimately giving them a city and surrounding land for their habitation.

l: Viriathus's assassination, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 5. The Lusitanians at first not having an expert general, were
s: After Ceepio repeatedly defeated Viriathus and Viriathus sued for peace, Ceepio caused Viriathus to be treacherously assassinated by some of his own servants.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: The unit describes Antiochus's siege of Jerusalem, his eventual pardon of the Jews, and the demolition of Jerusalem's walls. It recounts the servile war in Sicily, where abused slaves under Eunus and Cleon seized cities, defeated Roman forces, and were eventually suppressed by Rupilius. It also describes the Roman difficulties caused by the Cimbrians and several smaller slave rebellions in Italy, including one led by Titus Minutius at Capua.

l: Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Antiochus besieged Jerusalem, but after receiving hostages he pardoned the Jews, demolished the city's walls, and collected the tribute due. His friends urged him to destroy the Jews or abolish their laws, but he was described as generous and mild. Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes was also said to have entered the Jewish temple, sacrificed a swine there, defiled their books, extinguished their temple lamp, and compelled Jews to eat swine's flesh.

l: Jews, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: The Jews resisted Antiochus's siege until their provisions were exhausted, then sent ambassadors to negotiate. Antiochus received hostages and pardoned them, though their walls were demolished and their tribute collected.

l: Jerusalem, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Jerusalem was besieged by Antiochus. After the Jews surrendered hostages, Antiochus demolished the city's walls.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: During the siege, the Jews held out until their provisions were spent and then negotiated with Antiochus through ambassadors. The siege ended with their pardon, but Jerusalem's walls were destroyed.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Sicily prospered for sixty years after Carthage's overthrow, but its wealth and extensive use of slaves contributed to a major rebellion. The revolt spread across the island, with cities taken and Roman armies defeated, until Rupilius restored Roman control.

l: First Servile War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: The servile war began after Sicilian masters treated their slaves with extreme cruelty and failed to provide adequate food or clothing. Eunus and Cleon led large slave forces that defeated Roman commanders and captured cities, but Rupilius eventually defeated the rebels and cleared Sicily of them.

l: Sicilian slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: The Sicilian slaves were bought in large numbers, branded, used for shepherding and other labor, and harshly beaten while being denied necessities. They rebelled under Eunus and Cleon, killed many masters and other inhabitants, captured cities, and fought Roman forces before being suppressed.

l: Eunus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Eunus, a Syrian slave of Antigenes of Enna, claimed prophetic powers and used tricks to breathe fire from his mouth. He led the initial slave revolt, was made king under the name Antiochus, and ruled with an army that grew to many thousands. After Rupilius defeated the rebellion, Eunus fled into caves, was captured with four attendants, and died in prison at Morgantium, eaten by lice.

l: Enna, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Enna was the city where Eunus was enslaved and where the rebellion began. The rebels entered the city, massacred its inhabitants, and later held it against Rupilius until it was betrayed and captured after Cleon was killed.

l: Cleon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Cleon, a Cilician, led another slave uprising but joined forces with Eunus and served as his general with five thousand soldiers. He fought against the Romans and was killed while making a sortie from Enna; Rupilius then exposed his body and soon captured the city.

l: Roman generals, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Roman generals repeatedly fought the Sicilian rebels and were often defeated because of the rebels' superior numbers. Rupilius eventually recovered Taurominium, captured Enna, defeated the remaining rebels, and cleared Sicily of thieves and robbers.

l: Taurominium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Taurominium was recovered by Rupilius after a severe siege reduced its defenders to cannibalism. Rupilius captured Comaon, the brother of Cleon, while he was trying to escape, and Sarapion's betrayal of the citadel led to the capture and crucifixion of fugitives.

l: Rupilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Rupilius commanded the Roman campaign against the Sicilian slave revolt. He recovered Taurominium after a prolonged siege, captured Comaon, killed Cleon during a sortie from Enna, took Enna by betrayal, and later cleared Sicily of the remaining rebels.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: Rome was troubled by the Cimbrian successes in Gaul and by reports of the large slave rebellion in Sicily, having lost sixty thousand men in Gaul and lacking enough soldiers for a new expedition. Smaller slave conspiracies also occurred in Italy, and a rebellion of one hundred and fifty slaves began at Rome but was quickly suppressed.

l: Cimbrians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXIV.
s: The Cimbrians ravaged and harassed Gaul and inflicted many losses on the Romans. Rome had lost sixty thousand men in the war against them while also facing the Sicilian slave rebellion.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: The unit recounts the rise and suppression of a major slave rebellion in Sicily, beginning with revolts against Licinius Nerva and expanding under Salvius, Athenion, and Tryphon. The fugitive slaves captured territory, defeated Roman forces, besieged Morgantium and Lilybaeum, and established Tricala as a royal seat. Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Caius Aquilius led Roman campaigns against the rebels, with Aquilius eventually killing Athenion and ending the resistance. The account states that the servants' war lasted almost four years.

l: Lucius Licinius Lucullus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Lucius Licinius Lucullus was appointed by the senate to suppress the Sicilian rebels. He entered Sicily with a large army, defeated Tryphon and Athenion near Scirthsea, and pursued the fugitives to Tricala, but failed to take the place and was later brought to judgment and banished for neglecting his duty.

l: fugitive slaves, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: The fugitive slaves first gained strength through revolts across Sicily, often killing their masters and seizing strongholds. They defeated Roman forces, captured arms and prisoners, expanded into an army of tens of thousands, established kings, occupied territory, and fought Rome for almost four years before being defeated.

l: Roman army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: The Roman army fought repeatedly against the rebel slaves in Sicily. Roman forces sometimes suffered defeats, including the loss of arms at the battle near Mount Cyprianus and the defeat near Morgantium, but later campaigns under Lucullus and Caius Aquilius broke the rebellion.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Rome directed military campaigns against the Sicilian slave rebellion and appointed generals including Lucullus, Servilius, and Aquilius. Roman authorities also ordered captured rebels brought to Rome, where they were condemned to fight wild beasts.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Sicily was the principal setting of the slave rebellion and suffered widespread disorder, plunder, and violence. The revolt spread through many territories, including those of Morgantium, Aegesta, and Lilybaeum, before being suppressed by Roman forces.

l: Licinius Nerva, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Licinius Nerva, the Roman praetor or proconsul in Sicily, initially set more than eight hundred people free under a Roman decree. After pressure from local magistrates, he stopped freeing them and sent petitioners back to their masters, helping provoke the slave conspiracy; his later military efforts against the rebels were unsuccessful.

l: Salvius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Salvius, a fortune-teller, was chosen king by the rebellious slaves and later took the name Tryphon. He organized the army into three divisions, expanded its cavalry and infantry through raids, defeated a Roman army near Morgantium, and proclaimed liberty to the slaves there.

l: Morgantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Morgantium was a strong and well-fortified city besieged by Salvius and the rebels. A Roman general attempted to relieve it by attacking the rebel camp, but the rebels routed his army; the siege was later raised after the city's slaves fought in its defense.

l: Athenion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Athenion, a Cilician slave and skilled astrologer, became leader and then king of a separate rebel force in the territories of Aegesta and Lilybaeum. He later cooperated with Tryphon, was temporarily seized by him, and was released when Lucullus entered Sicily; during the battle near Scirthsea he wounded many Romans but was himself wounded and forced to flee. Caius Aquilius eventually fought and killed him.

l: Tryphon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Tryphon was the name taken by Salvius after he became king. He made Tricala his royal seat, summoned Athenion as his general, later suspected and seized him, and led the rebels against Lucullus; after the Roman victory near Scirthsea, Tryphon fled and later died.

l: Tricala, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Tricala was a strongly fortified place that Tryphon developed into the royal seat of the rebels. He strengthened its defenses, built a palace and marketplace, established a council and courts, and made it the center of the rebellion; Roman forces later besieged it but withdrew after suffering losses.

l: Caius Aquilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: Caius Aquilius was appointed general against the rebels after becoming consul with Caius Marius. He decisively defeated the remaining rebels, fought Athenion hand to hand and killed him, was wounded on the head, and pursued the survivors until their resistance was broken.

l: First Servile War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The care and management of the business for the reducing and
s: The First Servile War is represented in this unit as the Sicilian servants' war led successively by Salvius, Athenion, and Tryphon. It involved the capture of cities, widespread raids, and repeated battles with Roman forces, and ended after Caius Aquilius defeated the rebels; the account says it lasted almost four years.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The unit describes the Marsian war between the Romans and Italians, including the Italian attempt to establish a rival government called Italy and its eventual defeat. It then recounts seditions and civil wars in Rome involving Sylla, Marius, Caesar, Pompey, Brutus, Cassius, Antonius, and Augustus. It also explains the alleged Egyptian origin of the Jews, the foundation of Judea and Jerusalem under Moses, and the organization of Jewish laws and religious government. The unit concludes with an account of how fragments of Diodorus Siculus were collected and published.

l: Marsian War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Marsian war began after the Italians became dissatisfied with Roman promises of citizenship and enfranchisement. The Samnites, Asculans, Lucanians, Picenians, the people of Nola, and other communities fought against the Romans, but the Romans eventually prevailed. The Italians later abandoned their city and continued the struggle from Aesernia before the war ended.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Romans fought the Italians in a long and uncertain war, eventually regaining their former power and sovereignty. They were aided by commanders including Cneius Pompeius, Sylla, and Caius Cossius. Their later internal conflicts brought power first to Sylla and ultimately to Julius Caesar and Augustus.

l: Italians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Italians rebelled against Rome after repeated promises of citizenship were not fulfilled. They organized a rival government, divided Italy between their consuls, and called their new city Italy. After suffering repeated defeats and losing allies, they abandoned the city and moved to Aesernia.

l: Quintus Pompoedius Silo, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Quintus Pompoedius Silo, a Marsian of high standing, was chosen as one of the Italian consuls. He commanded the northern and western division of Italy and later led the remaining Italians from Aesernia. In a battle against the Romans, he killed some opponents but lost more than six thousand of his own men.

l: Caius Apootua Motulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Caius Apootua Motulus was chosen as the other Italian consul because of his notable actions. He commanded the southern and eastern division of Italy. At about the same time, he took the city of Venusia in Apulia and carried away more than three thousand prisoners.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Italians divided Italy into two regions for the exercise of their consular authority. They organized its government according to what they regarded as the ancient Roman model and called their new city Italy.

l: Cneius Pompeius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Cneius Pompeius was made consul and general during the Marsian war. Together with Sylla, who had been deputed by the other consul, he repeatedly routed the Italians and helped reduce their power.

l: Lucius Sylla, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Sylla helped Cneius Pompeius defeat the Italians and later compelled neighboring territories and cities to obey the Romans. He opposed Marius in a Roman civil war, prevailed, and became dictator. He later fought in Asia against Mithridates and ultimately gained control over Rome's political affairs.

l: Mithridates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Mithridates was asked by the Italians to invade Italy and oppose Rome. He replied that he would march into Italy after subduing Asia, where he was then engaged. His answer deprived the Italians of the assistance and financial support they hoped to receive.

l: Caius Julius Caesar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Caius Julius Caesar opposed Gaius Marius over the command of the expedition against Mithridates. Later, a conflict between Julius Caesar and Pompey involved Rome in further internal slaughter. Caesar's power eventually became unbounded after the restriction of consular authority.

l: Caius Marius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Gaius Marius, who had been consul six times, opposed Caius Julius Caesar over the command against Mithridates. He later fought Sylla, was defeated, and fled with fifteen thousand men to Praeneste. After being deserted and seeing no escape, he had himself killed by a faithful servant.

l: Marcus Antonius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Marcus Antonius, called Antonius in the account of the later civil war, managed the war against Brutus and Cassius together with Lepidus and Octavius Augustus. After that war, he entered into an open struggle with Augustus for supreme power and was defeated.

l: Octavius Augustus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Octavius Augustus helped conduct the war against Brutus and Cassius after Caesar's murder. He later fought Antonius for supreme power, prevailed, and held the empire throughout his life.

l: Pompey, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Pompey was called the Great because of his eminent services to the Romans, accomplished partly under Sylla and partly through his own valor. His conflict with Julius Caesar led to another civil war. After losing his army in a great battle, he was murdered near Alexandria.

l: Junius Brutus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Brutus was identified as one of Caesar's murderers. He fought the civil war conducted against him and Cassius by Lepidus, Antonius, and Octavius Augustus, and he died when that war ended.

l: Cassius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Cassius was identified as one of Caesar's murderers. He fought alongside Brutus against Lepidus, Antonius, and Octavius Augustus, and he died when that civil war was concluded.

l: Moses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Moses is described as the wise and valiant leader of the colony that settled in Judea. He possessed the country, built Jerusalem and its temple, instituted the worship of God, established laws, divided the people into twelve tribes, and organized their government and priesthood.

l: civil wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The unit describes several civil wars involving Marius and Sylla, Julius Caesar and Pompey, Brutus and Cassius against Antonius and Augustus, and Augustus against Antonius. These conflicts caused extensive slaughter and repeatedly changed who controlled Rome.

l: sedition in Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Sedition in Rome arose first from competition among Roman nobles for command of the war against Mithridates. A second great sedition was stirred up by Sylla and Marius, causing many thousands to perish. The account also connects later internal conflicts with the struggles between Caesar and Pompey and between Augustus and Antonius.

l: war against Mithridates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The war against Mithridates became the object of intense competition among Roman nobles because of the rewards and riches expected from it. Caius Julius Caesar and Gaius Marius disputed its command, while Sylla eventually led Roman forces in Asia against Mithridates.

l: war against the Jews, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The war against the Jews is introduced as the subject that follows the account of Roman civil conflicts. Before discussing it, the text says that the origin, laws, and customs of the Jewish nation should be explained.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Egypt is described as the setting of an ancient plague that some attributed to divine anger. The account says that many foreigners lived there and practiced foreign rites, which the native inhabitants believed had caused their religious customs to be neglected.

l: Egyptians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Egyptians concluded that their troubles would not end unless the foreigners were expelled. After the expulsion, the most valiant and noble among the displaced people traveled under skilled commanders to Greece and other places, while most settled in Judea.

l: Judea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Judea is described as the formerly deserted and uninhabited country where most of the expelled people settled. Moses led the colony there, established its institutions, and distributed its territories among the people.

l: Jerusalem, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Moses built Jerusalem and the temple there after taking possession of Judea. The city and temple are described as highly revered among the Jews.

l: Jews, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: The Jews are described as a people organized into twelve tribes under the laws attributed to Moses. The chief priest governed them as the messenger and interpreter of God's commands, and the people were expected to follow his declarations.

l: Jewish laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Jewish laws are attributed to Moses, who organized religious rites, government, inheritance, education, marriage, funerals, and military training. The laws prohibited the permanent sale of inherited land, encouraged the education of children, and gave priests larger portions so they could attend to worship.

l: God, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: God is described in the account as having no appropriate human image or representation. Moses is said to have taught that heaven, which surrounds the earth, was the only God and that all things were under its power.

l: Diodorus Siculus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXXVIL
s: Fragments attributed to Diodorus Siculus were collected under the direction of Constantine the seventh from works gathered into historical subject headings. The fragments in this collection came from the heading called Of Virtues and Vices and were published by Valesius.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: The unit recounts examples of virtue, impiety, justice, and good or bad government among figures including Lycurgus, Solon, Cyrus, and others. Lycurgus was highly esteemed, and while the Lacedaemonians observed his laws they became powerful and held sovereignty over Greece for more than four hundred years, but they lost that authority after neglecting the laws and embracing wealth and luxury. Solon was celebrated for wisdom, legislation, and virtue, and he helped turn the Athenians from luxury toward honorable conduct. Cyrus was distinguished for courage, prudence, and gentleness toward his subjects, while several other rulers and individuals suffered or were condemned for cruelty, treachery, or contempt of the gods.

l: Lycurgus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: Lycurgus was eminent for virtue, and the oracle at Delphos saluted him with verses. While the Lacedaemonians observed his laws, they rose from a low condition to great power and held sovereignty over Greece for more than four hundred years; when they neglected those laws and became slothful and luxurious, they lost their sovereign authority.

l: Solon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: Solon, an Athenian, was highly accomplished in wisdom and learning and was regarded as one of the seven wise men. He was honored for making laws and admired for his prudence in discourse, counsel, and advice; by degrees he turned the Athenians from luxurious and effeminate manners toward virtue and honorable actions.

l: Cyrus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: Cyrus, the son of Cambyses and Mandane and nephew of Astyages, excelled others of his age in courage, prudence, and other virtues. He was courageous against enemies and mild and gentle toward his subjects, for which the Persians called him their father; he also treated Croesus with honor and respect and made him one of his privy council.

l: virtue, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: Virtue is associated in the unit with courage, prudence, justice, piety, wisdom, gentleness, and honorable conduct. It brings honor and esteem to figures such as Lycurgus, Solon, Cyrus, and others, while the neglect of virtue is linked with luxury, tyranny, cruelty, and the loss of power.

l: impiety and contempt of the gods, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: Impiety and contempt of the gods are shown in figures such as Epopeus, Salmoneus, and Romulus Sylvius, who challenged, dishonored, or mocked the gods. Their conduct is presented as bringing destruction or divine punishment: Epopeus destroyed temples and altars, Salmoneus rejected sacrifices and imitated Jupiter's thunder, and Romulus Sylvius was struck dead by a thunderbolt.

l: laws and good government, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, *BOOKVI.
s: The unit presents laws and good government as foundations of strength, order, and public welfare. The Lacedaemonians became powerful while observing Lycurgus's laws but declined after neglecting them; Solon gained the Athenians toward virtue through laws and discipline; and Pittacus is praised as a prudent lawmaker who freed his country from tyranny, sedition, and war.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The unit describes Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans, emphasizing their eloquence, discipline, mutual aid, memory exercises, abstinence, and moral teachings. It recounts examples of friendship and loyalty involving Phintias and Damon, and explains how Lysis instructed Epaminondas in virtue through Pythagorean philosophy. The unit then presents examples of tyranny, courage, chastity, and public virtue involving Cambyses, Hipparchus, Hippias, Harmodius, Aristogiton, Zeno of Elea, Sextus Tarquinius, Lucretia, Hippocrates of Gela, and Cimon.

l: Pythagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Pythagoras flourished at Athens in the sixty-first Olympiad and was said to have been born at Samos, though some said Tyrrhenum. He was renowned for eloquence, gravity, sobriety, and persuading people to reject luxury; he cared for his former teacher Pherecydes on Delos, buried him, and returned to Italy. He taught his disciples to avoid unnecessary oaths, keep sworn promises, practice moderation, maintain bodily and spiritual purity, and cultivate virtue.

l: Pythagorean philosophy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Pythagorean philosophy provided Epaminondas with principles of patience, frugality, and other virtues through the instruction of Lysis.

l: Pythagoreans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The Pythagoreans supported members of their society who fell into poverty, even when they had never met them, and sometimes risked their lives for one another. They practiced memory exercises, abstinence, moderation, and moral purity, and were highly esteemed by the Crotonians.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Pythagoras sailed from Italy to Delos to care for Pherecydes and later returned to Italy. Clinlias also traveled from Italy to Cyrene to aid the impoverished Pythagorean Proran.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Dionysius the Tyrant used a scheme to threaten Phintias with execution, but was astonished when Damon agreed to serve as hostage. After Phintias returned at the appointed time, Dionysius pardoned him and wished to join the Pythagorean society.

l: Damon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Damon, a Pythagorean and pupil of Phintias, agreed without hesitation to become hostage and die in Phintias's place. He remained prepared for execution until Phintias returned at the last moment.

l: Crotona, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The Crotonians revered Pythagoras as if he were a god. One wealthy citizen of Crotona, Cylo, became hostile to the Pythagoreans after they rejected him.

l: Lysis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Lysis, a Pythagorean who went to Thebes in Boeotia, became tutor to Epaminondas and instructed him in virtue. Because of his excellent qualities, Lysis adopted Epaminondas as his son.

l: Epaminondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Epaminondas learned from Lysis and from the sparks of knowledge gained through Pythagorean philosophy. He consequently surpassed the Thebans and other Greeks of his time in patience, frugality, and other virtues.

l: virtue, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The unit presents virtue as cultivated through learning, sobriety, constancy, courage, patience, frugality, loyalty, and purity. It says that virtuous actions preserve a person's reputation and memory more lasting than monuments.

l: Cambyses, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Cambyses was described as furious, mad, fierce, and insolent. After taking Memphis and Pelusium, he desecrated and ordered the burning of the embalmed body of Amasis, and he ordered an army to plunder and burn the temple of Jupiter Ammon.

l: Hipparchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Hipparchus, brother of Thessalus and Hippias, ruled the Athenians tyrannically. His love for a beautiful boy placed him in peril and contributed to the conspiracy formed by Harmodius and Aristogiton.

l: Hippias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Hippias, brother of Thessalus and Hipparchus, is described as rigid and cruel. He ruled tyrannically over the Athenians with his brother.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The Athenians were grievously oppressed by the tyrannical rule of Hipparchus and Hippias.

l: Harmodius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Harmodius joined Aristogiton in a conspiracy against Hipparchus to free their country from slavery.

l: Aristogiton, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Aristogiton joined Harmodius in conspiring against Hipparchus. He was especially notable for a brave and resolute spirit, patience under torture, faithfulness to friends, and just revenge against enemies.

l: Athenian tyranny, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The Athenian tyranny is represented through the rigid and cruel rule of Hipparchus and Hippias, whose oppression led Harmodius and Aristogiton to conspire for the liberation of their country.

l: Zeno of Elea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Zeno of Elea was tortured after being seized for conspiring against the tyrant Nearchus. He endured the rack, then deceived Nearchus into approaching him and bit the tyrant's ear, refusing to release it until the guards begged him to do so.

l: Lucius Tarquinius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Roman Tarquinius is identified as the king of the Romans and the father of Sextus Tarquinius.

l: Sextus Tarquinius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Sextus Tarquinius went to Collatia and attempted to force Lucretia, threatening her with death and falsely framing her as an adulteress unless she yielded. He promised her rewards and marriage, but his violation led Lucretia to summon her household and take her own life.

l: Lucius Tarquinius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Lucius Tarquinius, the king's nephew, was Lucretia's husband. He was away with the army at Ardea when Sextus Tarquinius attacked her.

l: Lucretia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Lucretia was renowned for chastity and was attacked by Sextus Tarquinius while her husband was away. After Sextus left, she summoned her servants, denounced his violation of friendship and hospitality, and stabbed herself with a dagger.

l: suicide, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: The unit describes Lucretia's suicide after Sextus Tarquinius violated her chastity, presenting her death as an act connected to her concern for honor.

l: Hippocrates of Gela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Hippocrates of Gela rebuked the chief priests and citizens of Syracuse for plundering Jupiter's temple. He ordered them to return the sacred objects and did not take any of them himself, seeking both to preserve his reputation and to turn the people against Syracuse's oppressive governors.

l: Cimon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. When Thericles was chief magistrate at Athens in the sixty^
s: Cimon surrendered himself to imprisonment to pay his father's fine so that he could receive and bury his father's body. He later became a distinguished civil magistrate and a famous general, performing actions worthy of remembrance.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The unit describes the ambitions, actions, and reputations of several Hellenistic rulers and historians, especially Agathocles, Lysimachus, Dromichaetes, Demetrius, and Apollodorus. Dromichaetes captures Lysimachus but treats him generously, while Seleucus rejects a proposal to kill the imprisoned Demetrius. The text condemns Timaeus and Callias for distorting their histories of Agathocles, in opposite directions. It also recounts the massacres and seizures carried out by the Mamertines and Campanians, the cruelty of Apollodorus, and Pyrrhus’s failure to punish Gauls who plundered royal tombs.

l: Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Agathocles massacred nearly two thousand Ligurians and Tyrrhenians after they mutinously attacked his son Archagathus over their pay. Timaeus accused him of many invented crimes and minimized his successes, although the text says Agathocles was a prudent and expert general who rose from humble circumstances to rule Sicily and conquer parts of Italy and Africa. Callias, having been enriched and advanced by Agathocles, praised him excessively despite his violations of divine and human laws.

l: Thracians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The Thracians who captured Agathocles, son of Lysimachus, returned him to his father with gifts, hoping for protection and the restoration of their territory. Thracian soldiers initially demanded that the captive Lysimachus be put to death, but agreed with Dromichaetes that preserving him would serve the public good.

l: Lysimachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Lysimachus was captured by Dromichaetes and treated with civility, including being brought with his children into Helis. Dromichaetes released his friends and servants to him, entertained him at a banquet, and sought through this treatment to obtain the return of forts and castles formerly belonging to the Thracians.

l: Dromichaetes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Dromichaetes, king of Thrace, captured Lysimachus but argued successfully against killing him. He treated Lysimachus generously, returned his friends and servants, and used a carefully arranged banquet to persuade him that a Macedonian supper was preferable to a Thracian one.

l: Demetrius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: After forcing the remaining rebels into submission, King Demetrius pardoned all but fourteen leading Boeotian insurgents. While Demetrius was imprisoned at Pella, Lysimachus urged Seleucus to kill him, but Seleucus rejected the proposal and considered releasing him and restoring him to his kingdom.

l: Timaeus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Timaeus criticized earlier historians but was said to have forged many statements about Agathocles because Agathocles had banished him from Sicily. He minimized Agathocles’s successes, exaggerated his misfortunes, and repeatedly called him cowardly despite Agathocles’s military achievements; the text therefore condemns his history as biased and unreliable.

l: Callias, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Callias, a Syracusan enriched and advanced by Agathocles, praised him far beyond his merits. He portrayed Agathocles as exceptionally pious and righteous even though Agathocles had violated divine and human laws.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The Syracusans agreed with the mercenary soldiers, who then departed and were received by the Messenians as friends and allies. The text also notes the inconsistency in Timaeus’s praise of Syracusan valor while he called Agathocles, who conquered them, the greatest coward.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Sicily was the island from which Agathocles was banished by Timaeus. Agathocles later gained sovereign power over all Sicily.

l: Mamertines, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The Mamertines were mercenary soldiers who, after agreeing with the Syracusans, were received by the Messenians as friends and confederates. They then murdered their hosts, took their wives, and seized the city.

l: Messenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The Messenians received the Mamertines as friends and confederates. The Mamertines murdered them, took their wives, and seized their city.

l: Seleucus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Seleucus sharply rebuked Lysimachus’s ambassadors for asking him to kill the imprisoned Demetrius, because doing so would violate faith and commit a wicked act against a relative. He wrote to his son Antiochus for advice, although he had resolved to release Demetrius and restore him honorably to his kingdom.

l: Decius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Decius, a Campanian governor of the garrison at Rhegium, participated in the treacherous seizure of the city and sold the goods of its inhabitants. After he was expelled by the Campanian soldiers, a physician from Rhegium later blinded him with an eye treatment made from cantharides.

l: Campanians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The Campanian soldiers placed in charge of the garrison at Rhegium imitated the Mamertines by killing the Rhegians, taking their goods, and possessing themselves of the city. They later expelled Decius, their governor and accomplice in the crime.

l: Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Rhegium was occupied by Campanian soldiers who murdered its inhabitants and seized their property. Decius was later expelled from the city, and a physician from Rhegium took revenge on him by blinding him.

l: Apollodorus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Apollodorus sought sovereign power and sacrificed a young friend to confirm conspirators in their undertaking, giving them the victim’s entrails and mixing his blood with wine. He armed Gauls as a bodyguard, confiscated and sold the property of wealthy citizens, increased soldiers’ pay, distributed money to the poor, and extorted wealth through torture.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Apollodorus armed Gauls and employed them as his life-guard because they were considered naturally cruel and willing to carry out villainous acts. Pyrrhus later left a Gaulish garrison at Aegae, whose soldiers plundered the royal tombs and scattered the bones and ashes of the dead.

l: Pyrrhus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: After plundering Aegae, the royal seat of the Macedonian kings, Pyrrhus left a garrison of Gauls there. Although he was criticized when the Gauls opened the royal tombs and divided the treasures, he did not punish them because he used them in his wars.

l: capture of Lysimachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Dromichaetes captured Lysimachus, king of Thrace, and treated him and his children with civility. He persuaded the Thracians to preserve Lysimachus and used his release and generous treatment to seek the restoration of Thracian forts and castles.

l: massacre and seizure of Messana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The Mamertines were received by the Messenians as friends but murdered their hosts at night, took their wives, and seized Messana. The Campanian seizure of Rhegium is presented as a similar act of treachery.

l: history, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: The unit presents history as a discipline that should proclaim the truth. It condemns historians who distort the record through personal resentment or gratitude, particularly Timaeus’s attacks on Agathocles and Callias’s excessive praise of him.

l: Timaeus's bias against Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, FROM THE SAME..
s: Timaeus’s hostility toward Agathocles arose after Agathocles banished him from Sicily. The text says that Timaeus invented accusations, reduced Agathocles’s successes, magnified his accidental misfortunes, and falsely portrayed a capable and courageous commander as a coward.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: The unit condemns Attilius Regulus for rejecting an honourable and advantageous peace with the Carthaginians and for insulting them in their distress. Xantippos then led the Carthaginians to rout and destroy the Roman army, suddenly reversing the course of the war. The resulting conflict continued for fifteen years and included destructive sea-fights in which about one hundred thousand men perished. Amilcar Barcas and his son Hannibal are described as among the greatest generals, whose victories greatly enlarged Carthaginian territory.

l: Attilius Regulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Attilius Regulus is condemned for pride, folly, madness, and insolence. Although he could have concluded an honourable and advantageous peace for the Romans, he imposed unreasonable conditions on the Carthaginians, provoking them to continue the war; he later suffered defeat, dishonour, and the scorn of those whom he had previously mocked.

l: Xantippos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Xantippos delivered the Carthaginians from their immediate dangers and completely changed the course of affairs. He routed the recently victorious Romans after a great slaughter, and his prudence and wisdom were credited with overcoming the difficulties facing the Carthaginians.

l: Amilcar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Amilcar, called Barcas, is described as one of the greatest generals to have appeared before or after his time. His victories greatly enlarged the dominions of the Carthaginians.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Hannibal is identified as the son of Amilcar Barcas and is described, with his father, as one of the greatest generals to have appeared before or after them. Their victories greatly enlarged the dominions of the Carthaginians.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: The Romans were initially victorious and were regarded as the best soldiers in the world, but Xantippos routed and cut off their army. After this defeat, they were so distressed and amazed that they no longer dared to engage the enemy in the same manner and were later confined to a small town.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: The Carthaginians were initially terrified, closely besieged, and expecting destruction, but Xantippos restored their courage and led them to defeat the Romans. They were thereby raised from near ruin to such prosperity that they later slighted and contemned their enemy.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Rome was thrown into distress and amazement after the Roman army's defeat. Although its soldiers had previously been regarded as the world's best, the city saw them lose confidence in confronting the enemy.

l: peace between Rome and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Attilius Regulus could have concluded a peace that would have been honourable and advantageous to the Romans but base and dishonourable to the Carthaginians. He rejected that opportunity and instead demanded unreasonable conditions.

l: Attilius's defeat, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Attilius's defeat followed his refusal to show clemency and humanity toward the distressed Carthaginians. His army was routed and cut off, and his resulting dishonour and disgrace outweighed his former glory and reputation.

l: Roman defeat by Xantippos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: Xantippos's defeat of the Romans produced a sudden reversal of the war. The Romans, who had recently been conquerors and masters of sea and land, were routed after a prodigious slaughter and confined to a small town.

l: sea-fights, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: The conflict came to be decided by sea-fights involving a vast number of Roman and allied ships. Many ships were destroyed, and one hundred thousand men perished in these battles.

l: the war between Rome and Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIII.
s: The war between Rome and Carthage became the longest war recorded from former times, continuing for fifteen years. After the Roman defeat by Xantippos, it involved major sea-fights and required immense expenditure to maintain the fleet.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Clodius took command of the Roman army besieging Lilybsum and criticized his predecessors, but acted rashly, punished soldiers severely, and was arrogant about his birth. Amilcar is praised as a courageous, prudent, industrious, and ambitious Carthaginian general. Hanno captured Hecatompylos, spared the city after taking three thousand hostages, and was rewarded with the inhabitants' hospitality. The wife of Attilius cruelly confined the captives, causing Bostar's death, until the magistrates intervened, punished the Attilii, and freed Amilcar.

l: Clodius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Clodius took command of the army besieging Lilybsum and bitterly accused the consuls who had preceded him of mismanaging the war. He rashly attempted to build a mole in the sea to block the harbor, severely punished soldiers, scourged Roman allies, and despised others because of his noble birth and ancestry.

l: Roman soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: The Roman soldiers received a harsh commander in Clodius, who punished them severely and accused their former leaders of allowing them to indulge in wine, luxury, and pleasure.

l: siege of Lilybsum, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: The siege of Lilybsum was being conducted by a Roman army when Clodius arrived and assumed command. Clodius claimed that the Romans were more besieged than the enemy and attempted to block the harbor with a mole.

l: Amilcar (Carthaginian general), The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Amilcar was known before his appointment as a man of magnanimous spirit. As general, he lived up to expectations by pursuing fame, despising danger, and displaying prudence, courage, and industry.

l: Hanno, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Hanno was ambitious and hoped to use an idle army to train the soldiers, reduce the city's expenses, and win an honorable and profitable success. After taking Hecatompylos, he chose mercy over severity, preserved the city and its citizens' estates, and took three thousand hostages.

l: Hecatompylos, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Hecatompylos was captured by Hanno. Its city, citizens, and estates were preserved after its elders appealed to him for mercy.

l: hostages taken by Hanno, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Hanno took three thousand hostages after capturing Hecatompylos. The text later refers to captives who were confined and mistreated by the Attilius family.

l: Attilius's wife, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Attilius's wife blamed the young men for the death of her husband and urged them to treat the captives cruelly. She confined Amilcar with Bostar's corpse, gave Amilcar only enough food to keep him alive, and refused his pleas for compassion.

l: Attilius's sons, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Attilius's sons were urged by their mother to mistreat the captives because she believed their carelessness had caused their father's death. They confined the captives in a small room, where Bostar died after five days without food.

l: Bostar, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Bostar was one of the captives held in a cramped room by Attilius's sons. He died after five days without food from distress and starvation, and his body was later burned and his ashes sent back to his own country.

l: Attilii, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: The Attilii were held responsible for the cruel treatment of the captives and narrowly escaped being put to death. The magistrates threatened to punish them severely if they did not treat prisoners humanely in the future.

l: magistrates of Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: The magistrates were informed of the captives' mistreatment by the tribunes of the people. They summoned the Attilii, threatened them with severe punishment, attributed much of the cruelty to their mother, arranged for Bostar's body to be burned, and freed Amilcar.

l: Amilcar's imprisonment, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Amilcar was confined in a small, foul room with Bostar's corpse and was deprived of food except what was necessary to keep him alive. He prayed to Jupiter and the other gods for vengeance, but was eventually discovered and freed after servants reported his condition.

l: Bostar's death, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: Bostar died after being confined without food for five days, overcome by mental anguish and famine. The magistrates had his body burned and sent the ashes back to his own country.

l: the captives' confinement, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXIV.
s: The captives were thrust into a small enclosed room and forced to crowd together like beasts. They were kept without food for five days, resulting in Bostar's death, while Amilcar endured further confinement with the corpse until the authorities intervened.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: The Carthaginians, after twenty-four years of war with the Romans for Sicily, were driven into severe distress when their mercenary soldiers revolted after being denied their pay. Spondius and the other rebel captains refused the Carthaginians permission to bury their dead and ordered cruel punishments for prisoners. Amilcar retaliated against the rebels by having captives tortured and trampled by elephants. The Hippacrineans and Uticans also revolted, while Amilcar later gained great honors and was briefly made general of all Libya after the war in Africa ended.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: The Carthaginians had been at war with the Romans for twenty-four years over possession of Sicily. They attempted to defraud their mercenary soldiers of their pay, after which the mercenaries revolted and brought them into severe distress. They requested permission to bury their dead, but the rebels refused, and they later retaliated against prisoners.

l: mercenary soldiers, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: The mercenary soldiers were denied their pay by the Carthaginians and consequently revolted. They brought Carthage into miserable distress and, under their captains, adopted cruel measures against Carthaginian prisoners and confederates.

l: revolt of the mercenaries, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: The revolt began when the Carthaginians attempted to defraud their mercenary soldiers of their pay. It threatened the Carthaginians with the loss of both their sovereign authority and their country, and it was accompanied by severe cruelty on both sides.

l: Spondius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: Spondius, one of the captains of the revolters, refused the Carthaginians permission to bury those slain in battle and warned them not to send further messengers. He ordered that captured Carthaginians be put to death and that captured confederates have their hands cut off and be sent back to Carthage.

l: Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: Africa was the setting of the war against the mercenaries and Libyans after the conflict with the Romans in Sicily. After that war ended, Amilcar was briefly made general of all Libya.

l: war in Africa against the mercenaries and Libyans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXV.
s: The war in Africa involved the Carthaginians fighting the mercenaries and the Libyans, who had revolted and closely besieged Carthage itself. Amilcar performed notable actions in the war with great valor and prudence, and the war eventually ended.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: This unit describes Hannibal's military character, his conduct toward Roman captives, and his actions in Italy and Africa during the conflict with Rome. It recounts Scipio's humane treatment of Syphax and the Carthaginian ambassadors, as well as the fall of Syracuse and the punishment of Roman and Carthaginian offenders. It also reports the misconduct and misfortunes of Philip of Macedon and Antiochus, including their attacks on temples and defeats. The unit praises Roman fidelity to treaties and clemency while attributing the downfall of impious rulers to divine vengeance.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
