s: Hannibal is described as naturally warlike and highly experienced through long military service. His army in Campania became weakened by luxury, and he later forced those who wished to remain in Italy to surrender captives and put twenty thousand infantry and three thousand cavalry to death. He showed respect for Sempronius Gracchus after his death, sent his bones and ashes to the Roman camp, and later crossed into Africa.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: The Romans are praised for their piety, patience, and constancy when Hannibal forced captive relatives to fight one another; none would attack a friend or family member. Their ambassadors were nearly killed by Carthaginians but were saved by Scipio, who also released captured Carthaginian ambassadors rather than retaliating. The Romans are said to have begun wars only on just principles and to have honored their leagues and oaths.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: The Carthaginians are condemned for Hannibal's cruel treatment of Roman captives and for attempting to throw Roman ambassadors overboard. They severely punished the Micatanian Numidians, crucifying their captives and creating lasting enmity. Their people also sent ambassadors to negotiate with Scipio after the conflict.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: After Hieronymus was killed, Syracuse decreed that all of the tyrant's relatives, men and women, should be put to death. When Syracuse was taken, its citizens approached Marcellus with olive branches, and he promised to spare the lives of its freemen while allowing their property to be taken by his soldiers.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: Hannibal's army spent a long period in Campania, where luxury and indulgence weakened its bodies and courage. Hannibal later provided shipping for those who would leave Italy, while those who remained were surrounded and largely killed or taken captive.

l: Scipio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: Scipio treated Syphax humanely, freeing him from chains, giving him his tent, and allowing him considerable liberty. He refused to retaliate against Carthaginian ambassadors for the attempted murder of Roman ambassadors. He also imprisoned Pleminius after the sacrilege at the temple of Proserpina and was ordered to return to Rome if he had directed or contrived the offense.

l: Rome, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: Rome received the Locrians' appeal concerning Pleminius's plunder of the temple of Proserpina. Its senate sent representatives to investigate Scipio's responsibility, imprisoned Pleminius, devoted his goods to Proserpina, and ordered compensation from the public treasury for any deficiency. Rome also declared that the Locrians should be free.

l: Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: Philip of Macedon encouraged piracy, supported attacks on merchants and islands, and was influenced by Heraclides to execute senators and undertake unnecessary wars. He plundered temples, sepulchres, and places in Attica and around Pergamas, becoming widely hated. After suffering defeat and nearly losing his kingdom, he was preserved by Roman clemency.

l: Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: Antiochus was condemned for attacking Roman soldiers in peacetime, neglecting military affairs for luxury, and abandoning Lysimachia, which later aided Scipio's army. He also robbed the temple of Jupiter Belus in Elymais after pretending that its inhabitants had made war against him, and the text says the gods soon took vengeance for this sacrilege. After a defeat, he became disheartened and resolved to abandon Europe.

l: Hannibal's war in Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XXVI.
s: The Roman-Carthaginian war is represented through Hannibal's campaigns, the treatment of Roman captives, Scipio's dealings with Syphax and the Carthaginian ambassadors, and Hannibal's eventual return to Africa. The unit contrasts Carthaginian cruelty and attempted retaliation with Roman clemency, treaty-keeping, and restraint.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: The unit concerns Hannibal's skill as a general and his command of a diverse army. Hannibal maintained his army's discipline without mutinies, despite differences in nationality, temperament, and language. He led large armies through Italy for seventeen years without lacking money or provisions, defeating powerful nations and winning every battle described. His campaigns destroyed cities and almost depopulated Italy, while his strategy overcame forces strengthened by foreign auxiliaries and allies.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: Hannibal was the most expert general and undertook the greatest enterprises of any of the Carthaginians. Through prudent conduct, he kept his army obedient and disciplined, won every battle he fought, devastated much of Italy, and overcame numerically strong enemies through policy and military stratagems.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: The Carthaginians included Hannibal, who was said to have undertaken their greatest enterprises. Those of Hannibal's own nation were accustomed on slight occasions to desert and go over to the enemy, but none under his command dared attempt it.

l: Hannibal's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: Hannibal's army included soldiers differing greatly in temperament and language, including foreigners and mercenaries. It experienced no mutinies, remained in orderly discipline, and had sufficient money and provisions despite marching from place to place with very large forces.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: Italy was wasted and harassed by Hannibal for seventeen years. Many of its cities were laid in ashes after being taken by storm, and the country was almost depopulated.

l: battles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: Hannibal was victorious in every battle he fought in this account. His battles caused terrible slaughter among people reputed to be the leaders of the world, so that none dared face him or engage him in battle.

l: Hannibal's war in Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: Hannibal's war in Italy lasted seventeen years and was directed against the most powerful nations. It wasted and harassed almost all Italy, destroyed many cities, and relied on Hannibal's disciplined forces and military stratagems.

l: military discipline, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 3G. Hannibal was the most expert general, and p^rfgnoed dm
s: Military discipline in Hannibal's army was maintained through his prudent conduct, even though the soldiers differed in nationality, temperament, and language. The unit presents this discipline as a major reason he achieved greater and more renowned actions.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: P. Scipio defeated the Carthaginians, compelled Hannibal to leave Italy, and finally overcame him and brought Carthage under Roman rule. The unit describes Perseus's failures, including his refusal to pay the Gauls, his loss of Macedonia, and his eventual captivity and death. It praises Tiberius Gracchus and Paulus Æmilius, contrasts Eumenes's generosity with Perseus's covetousness, and recounts Antiochus III's erratic conduct and Ptolemy's weakness. It also emphasizes Roman clemency toward defeated peoples, including the liberation of the Macedonian cities and favorable treatment of the Macedonians and Illyrians.

l: Scipio, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: While still very young, P. Scipio performed great things in Spain beyond general expectation. He defeated the Carthaginians, delivered his country from imminent dangers, compelled Hannibal to leave Italy without fighting, and later overcame him in battle, bringing Carthage under Roman rule.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Carthaginians were defeated by P. Scipio in Spain and elsewhere, and their defeat helped deliver Rome from imminent dangers.

l: Hannibal, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Hannibal could not be overcome by force of arms, but P. Scipio compelled him to leave Italy without fighting. Scipio later defeated him in a great battle.

l: Carthage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Carthage was brought under the Roman yoke after P. Scipio defeated Hannibal.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Romans conquered Macedonia after many battles and great dangers, but treated the defeated peoples with clemency. They proclaimed liberty to the cities of Macedonia, allowed the Illyrians to use their own laws, and imposed only half the tribute that the Macedonians and Illyrians had paid to their kings.

l: Perseus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Perseus repeatedly acted with negligence, covetousness, and poor judgment. He refused to pay the Gauls who had come to assist him, lost their support, ordered treasure and ships destroyed, removed the inhabitants of Dion to Pydna, and was eventually conquered by the Romans, confined with a keeper, and brought to a miserable end.

l: Tiberius Gracchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Tiberius Gracchus managed the war in Spain vigorously despite his youth, excelling men of his age in courage and prudence. He later arrived as an ambassador to inspect the affairs of Syria and was received with great kindness by Antiochus III, without suspecting the king's hostile designs toward Rome.

l: Paulus Æmilius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Paulus Æmilius was celebrated for his nobility, prudence, courage, and military skill. As consul and general in Macedonia, he encouraged the Roman legions, employed new stratagems, defeated the Macedonians, and later treated Perseus courteously and mercifully.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: The Macedonians were defeated by Paulus Æmilius and the Romans. The Romans nevertheless proclaimed them free, reduced their tribute to half of what they had paid their kings, and treated them with clemency.

l: Antiochus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Antiochus III displayed both admirable and contemptible conduct. He defeated the Egyptians but spared them and gained advantage through his humanity; he also behaved in an undignified and ridiculous manner at public games, while secretly remaining an enemy of the Romans.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Eumenes used bribery to gain Abdera through Python, who opened the gates but later repented when he saw the destruction of his country. Unlike Perseus, Eumenes paid his soldiers what they were owed, gave them additional gifts, and won their loyalty through generosity.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: A body of Gauls crossed the river Ister to assist Perseus, but their general demanded the promised payment of about five hundred talents. Because Perseus refused to pay, the Gauls returned home, causing him to lose their assistance; Eumenes later brought the whole nation of the Gauls into subjection.

l: Macedonia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Macedonia was conquered by the Romans after their battles with Perseus. Its cities were proclaimed free, and the Macedonians were required to pay only half the tribute they had paid to their kings.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, 37. P. Scipio, when he was but very young, performed great and
s: Ptolemy was condemned for surrendering his rich kingdom without a struggle when the enemy was still far away. His weakness was attributed to Eulaius, who had raised him from childhood in pleasures and womanish recreations; after being driven out, Ptolemy traveled toward Rome and declined Demetrius's offer of royal insignia.
